analysis.one_liner: Writes qualified immunity into federal law, shielding police officers and their agencies from damages lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a Republican with 34 Republican cosponsors, never received a committee vote or any floor action and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write the court-created doctrine of qualified immunity into federal civil rights law. Under that doctrine, a person who sues a police officer for violating their constitutional rights cannot win money damages unless the right in question was already "clearly established" at the time, meaning every reasonable officer would have known the conduct was illegal. The bill also says a police department or local government cannot be held liable if the individual officer is not liable. In practice, it would lock in the current legal standard that makes most civil rights damages lawsuits against officers fail.
analysis.who_benefits: Law enforcement officers sued in their individual capacity, plus the departments and local governments that employ them. Officers would gain a statutory shield from paying damages for rights violations unless the law was already unmistakably clear, and agencies would be immune from liability whenever the individual officer escapes it [S2] [S3]. Taxpayers in those jurisdictions would also be spared paying judgments, though at the cost of leaving rights violations uncompensated.

how_it_helps.text: Codifies the qualified immunity defense, so an officer cannot be found liable if the constitutional right was not "clearly established" at the time, or if a court had already upheld the specific conduct [S2] [S3].
Shields law enforcement agencies and local governments from liability whenever the individual officer is found not liable and was acting within the scope of employment [S2].
The bill's findings argue the doctrine protects officers from "harassment, distraction, and liability" for reasonable mistakes, which supporters say helps recruitment and retention [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People whose constitutional rights are violated by law enforcement officers. Because the "clearly established" standard defeats many otherwise valid claims even under current law, writing it into statute would leave victims of police misconduct with no damages remedy in a large share of cases, and departments could avoid liability entirely through the officer's individual immunity [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Under the "clearly established" standard, victims can lose even when the court agrees their rights were violated, simply because no earlier case had squarely ruled the same conduct illegal; the bill would entrench that standard in statute rather than leaving courts free to narrow it [S2] [S3].
The bill bars liability for the employing agency or local government whenever the officer individually escapes liability, removing any financial accountability at the departmental level [S2].

Supporters would counter that the doctrine, as the Supreme Court has described it, balances accountability against shielding officers who make reasonable mistakes, and that the bill simply preserves that settled balance rather than changing it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main practical effect would be to convert a court-made, changeable doctrine into a fixed statute, making it harder for courts to narrow qualified immunity over time. Departments and municipalities would save on judgments and settlements, but the cost falls on people injured by rights violations, many of whom would have no way to be compensated even when a court found their rights were actually violated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2021, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee two months later, and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Banks (R-IN), joined by Rep. Greg Steube, introduced the bill on January 13, 2021 [S1] [S3] [S5].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and on March 4, 2021 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded for the rest of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023 [S5].
The bill attracted 34 cosponsors, all Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement officers, police departments, and local governments are better off, since the qualified immunity shield they operate under was left intact by the courts rather than being codified but also never being weakened. Victims of police misconduct gained nothing from the bill's failure, because the existing immunity doctrine remains in place either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police officers, departments, and local governments

for.name: Rep. Jim Banks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Qualified Immunity Act of 2021 on January 13, 2021.

for.name: Rep. Greg Steube
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only named co-introducer.

for.name: 34 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after it was referred — no hearing, markup, or committee vote in two years.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 34 cosponsors were House Republicans; with Democrats holding the House majority in the 117th Congress, the Democratic-run Judiciary Committee never brought the bill to a vote.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and police departments
industries.note: The bill would lock the qualified immunity shield into statute, making officers and their agencies permanently harder to sue for damages after rights violations. It preserves the status quo that currently leaves most victims of police misconduct without compensation [S2] [S3].

By barring liability for the employing agency whenever the individual officer is not liable, the bill would spare local governments and their taxpayers from damages payouts, while the people harmed by misconduct bear the loss uncompensated [S2].

industries.industry: Police unions and law enforcement associations
industries.note: A statutory qualified immunity defense would protect their members from personal financial liability and reduce disciplinary and legal pressure from civil suits, aligning union interests against victims' ability to sue [S3].
Lawyers who represent people suing over police misconduct would see more cases dismissed under a codified, court-proof immunity standard, reducing both recoveries for clients and fee income.
